Press Up: Start in a high plank position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows, keeping them at roughly a 45-degree angle from your body. Pause briefly at the bottom, then push powerfully back up to the start position. Keep your core tight and avoid letting your hips sag or rise throughout the movement. Breathe in on the way down and out as you push up.
Wide Press Ups: Take a high plank position with your hands placed wider than shoulder-width apart, fingers pointing slightly outward. Lower your chest to the floor by bending your elbows out to the sides, keeping your body rigid and your core engaged. Push back up to the start position. The wider hand position places greater emphasis on the outer chest and shoulder muscles. Keep your neck neutral and avoid shrugging your shoulders.
Clock Push Up: Begin in a standard push-up position. Perform a push-up, then walk or jump your hands one position clockwise (imagine a clock face on the floor beneath you). Repeat the push-up and continue moving around the clock — 12, 3, 6, and 9 o'clock positions. This variation challenges shoulder stability, balance, and overall upper body coordination while hitting the chest from multiple angles.
Clock Push Ups: Begin in a standard push-up position. Perform a push-up, then walk or jump your hands one position clockwise (imagine a clock face on the floor beneath you). Repeat the push-up and continue moving around the clock — 12, 3, 6, and 9 o'clock positions. This variation challenges shoulder stability, balance, and overall upper body coordination while hitting the chest from multiple angles.
Bicep Curl: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, arms fully extended by your sides, palms facing forward. Keeping your upper arms completely still and pressed to your torso, curl the weights up toward your shoulders by contracting your biceps. Squeeze at the top for a brief pause, then slowly lower the dumbbells back to the start under full control. Avoid swinging your body or using momentum — the movement should be smooth and deliberate throughout.
Hammer Curls: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, arms by your sides, with your palms facing each other (neutral grip). Keeping your elbows tucked close to your torso, curl both dumbbells up simultaneously toward your shoulders. The neutral grip shifts more emphasis to the brachialis and brachioradialis muscles alongside the biceps. Squeeze at the top and lower slowly back to the start position. Keep your upper body still throughout.
Cross Body Hammer Curl: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral (hammer) grip. Curl one dumbbell diagonally across your body toward the opposite shoulder, keeping your elbow close to your side. Lower it slowly and repeat on the other side. The cross-body movement targets the brachialis and adds a rotational challenge. Alternate arms for each rep and maintain a straight, stable torso.
Bench Press: Lie flat on a bench with your feet firmly on the floor. Grip the barbell slightly wider than shoulder-width with your palms facing away. Unrack the bar and hold it directly above your chest with arms fully extended. Lower the bar in a controlled arc to mid-chest level, keeping your elbows at about 75 degrees from your torso. Pause briefly, then drive the bar back up powerfully to the start position. Keep your shoulder blades retracted and pressed into the bench throughout the lift.
Incline Bench Press: Set a bench to a 30-45 degree incline. Lie back with your feet flat on the floor and grip the barbell slightly wider than shoulder-width. Unrack the bar and lower it in a controlled manner to the upper portion of your chest, keeping your elbows angled outward. Press the bar back up to the starting position, fully extending your arms without locking out your elbows. The incline angle places extra emphasis on the upper chest and front deltoids.
Dumbbell Flys: Lie flat on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand, arms extended above your chest with a slight bend in the elbows and palms facing each other. Slowly lower your arms out to the sides in a wide arc, feeling a deep stretch across your chest. Stop when your arms are roughly parallel to the floor, then squeeze your chest muscles to bring the dumbbells back up and together in the same arc. Maintain the slight elbow bend throughout and avoid using momentum.
Incline Dumbbell Flys: Set a bench to a 30-45 degree incline. Lie back holding a dumbbell in each hand with arms extended above your upper chest and palms facing each other, elbows slightly bent. Lower your arms out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a good stretch across the upper chest. Squeeze your chest to reverse the motion and bring the dumbbells back together above you. Keep the movement controlled and arc-like — this is not a pressing movement.
Dumbell Pullover: Lie across a flat bench with your upper back supported, feet flat on the floor. Hold a single dumbbell with both hands directly above your chest, arms slightly bent. Keeping your hips low and core tight, lower the dumbbell in an arc behind your head toward the floor, feeling a stretch through your chest and lats. Pull the weight back up and over to the starting position using your chest and lat muscles. Breathe in as you lower and out as you pull back.
Bench Dips: Sit on the edge of a sturdy bench with your hands gripping the edge beside your hips and fingers pointing forward. Slide your body off the bench so your weight is supported by your arms, with your legs extended in front of you. Bend your elbows and lower your body toward the floor until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the ground. Press back up by straightening your arms. Keep your back close to the bench and your chest up throughout the movement.
Tricep Extension: Stand or sit holding a dumbbell with both hands, arms extended overhead with the weight resting in your palms. Keeping your upper arms stationary and close to your head, bend your elbows and slowly lower the dumbbell behind your head until your forearms are roughly parallel to the floor. Extend your arms back up by contracting your triceps. Avoid flaring your elbows — keep them pointing forward throughout.
Incline Tricep Extension: Set a bench to a low-to-moderate incline (around 30 degrees). Lie back holding a dumbbell in each hand with arms extended above your chest, palms facing each other. Keeping your upper arms fixed and pointing upward, bend your elbows and lower the dumbbells toward the sides of your head. Extend your arms back to the start by squeezing your triceps. The incline changes the angle of resistance, adding variety to tricep development.
Tricep Kickbacks: Hold a dumbbell in one hand and place the opposite knee and hand on a bench for support, with your back parallel to the floor. Bring your working arm up so your upper arm is parallel to the floor and your elbow is bent at 90 degrees. Keeping your upper arm still, extend your forearm straight back by contracting your tricep until your arm is fully extended. Hold briefly, then slowly lower back to 90 degrees. Avoid swinging — use a controlled, deliberate motion.
Shoulder Press: Sit or stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height, palms facing forward. Press the dumbbells straight up above your head until your arms are fully extended but not locked out. Lower them back down under control to shoulder height. Keep your core tight and avoid arching your lower back. The shoulder press primarily targets the deltoids, with secondary work from the triceps and upper trapezius.
Lateral Raises: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with a slight bend in the elbows. With control, raise both arms out to the sides until they are parallel to the floor, forming a T shape. Pause briefly at the top, then slowly lower back to the start. Avoid swinging or using momentum — lead the movement with your elbows rather than your wrists. This exercise isolates the medial deltoids to build width in the shoulders.
Front Raises: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand resting in front of your thighs, palms facing your body. Keeping a slight bend in the elbows, raise one or both arms straight in front of you to shoulder height. Pause at the top, then lower slowly back to the start. The front raise primarily targets the anterior (front) deltoids. Avoid rocking backward as the weight comes up.
Flat Bench Lateral Raise: Lie on your side on a flat bench, supporting yourself with one arm. Hold a dumbbell in the top hand, arm extended down. Raise the dumbbell in a smooth arc upward until your arm is roughly perpendicular to the floor. Lower slowly back down. This variation isolates the lateral deltoid with gravity working directly against the movement, offering a unique challenge compared to standing lateral raises.
Shrugs: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, arms fully extended. Keeping your arms straight, elevate your shoulders as high as possible toward your ears. Hold the contraction briefly at the top, then lower slowly. Avoid rolling your shoulders. Shrugs primarily target the upper trapezius muscles of the upper back and neck.
One Arm Row: Place one knee and the same-side hand on a flat bench for support, with your back parallel to the floor. Hold a dumbbell in the opposite hand, arm extended straight down. Pull the dumbbell up toward your hip by retracting your shoulder blade and driving your elbow back, keeping it close to your body. Lower the weight slowly back to the start. The one-arm row targets the lats, rhomboids, and rear deltoids.
Incline Dumbbell Row: Set a bench to a moderate incline (30-45 degrees). Lie chest-down on the bench holding a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down. Row both dumbbells up simultaneously by retracting your shoulder blades and driving your elbows toward the ceiling. Squeeze at the top and lower slowly. The incline position removes momentum and provides a great stretch at the bottom, making this excellent for the middle and upper back.
Pull ups Knuckles Away: Grip a pull-up bar with your palms facing away from you (overhand grip), hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Hang with your arms fully extended. Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down toward your hips until your chin clears the bar. Lower yourself under full control back to the starting position. This standard pull-up primarily targets the lats, rhomboids, and biceps.
Pull ups Knuckles Towards: Grip a pull-up bar with your palms facing toward you (underhand grip), hands about shoulder-width apart. Hang with your arms fully extended. Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down and back until your chin clears the bar. Lower slowly back to the start. The underhand grip places more emphasis on the biceps while still heavily engaging the lats and upper back.
Sit Ups: Lie flat on your back with your knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Place your hands lightly behind your head or crossed on your chest. Engage your core and curl your torso up toward your knees, lifting your lower back off the floor. Pause briefly at the top, then lower yourself back down with control. Avoid pulling on your neck — let your abs do the work. Sit-ups target the rectus abdominis and hip flexors.
Weighted Sit Ups: Lie flat on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell across your chest or extended overhead. Perform a sit-up by curling your torso up toward your knees. The added resistance increases the challenge on the rectus abdominis. Lower yourself back slowly and with control. Keep the weight secure and stable throughout the movement.
Leg Raises: Lie flat on your back with your legs straight and your arms at your sides or gripping the sides of a bench for support. Keeping your legs together and as straight as possible, raise them toward the ceiling until they are perpendicular to the floor. Slowly lower them back down without letting your feet touch the floor. Leg raises effectively target the lower portion of the rectus abdominis and the hip flexors.
Weighted Leg Raises: Lie flat on your back and hold a dumbbell or weight between your feet. With legs kept as straight as possible, raise them toward the ceiling, then lower slowly without letting your feet touch the floor. The added weight intensifies the challenge on the lower abs and hip flexors. Brace your core and press your lower back gently into the floor throughout the movement.
Russian Twist: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet elevated slightly off the ground, leaning back at roughly a 45-degree angle. Clasp your hands together in front of your chest. Rotate your torso to the right, bringing your hands toward the floor beside your hip. Return to centre, then rotate to the left. Continue alternating sides in a controlled, rhythmic motion. This exercise targets the obliques and rotational core muscles.
Russian Twist with Weights: Perform the same movement as the Russian Twist but hold a dumbbell, weight plate, or medicine ball with both hands. The added load significantly increases the challenge for the obliques and overall core. Keep the rotation controlled and deliberate — avoid using momentum. Elevate your feet for a greater challenge.
Weighted Russian Twists: Sit on the floor with knees bent, feet lifted, and your torso angled back. Hold a dumbbell or weight plate with both hands in front of your chest. Rotate side to side, touching the weight to the floor on each side. Maintain a braced core and steady breathing throughout. The weighted version amplifies oblique activation and builds rotational strength and stability.
Plank: Begin in a forearm plank position with your elbows directly beneath your shoulders and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. Squeeze your glutes, brace your core, and hold the position. Avoid letting your hips sag toward the floor or rise into the air. Keep your neck neutral — look down at the floor. Breathe steadily throughout. The plank is a foundational exercise for building deep core stability and endurance.
Wipers: Lie flat on your back with your arms extended out to the sides for stability. Raise your legs straight up toward the ceiling so they are perpendicular to the floor. Keeping your legs together and as straight as possible, lower them slowly to one side until they are just above the floor. Use your obliques and core to bring them back up to centre, then lower to the other side. This movement targets the obliques, lower abs, and spinal rotators.
Squats: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and toes pointed slightly outward. Keeping your chest up and your back straight, push your hips back and bend your knees to lower yourself as if sitting into a chair. Descend until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, keeping your knees tracking over your toes. Drive through your heels to stand back up. Squats are a foundational compound movement targeting the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and core.
Lunges: Stand tall with your feet together. Step one foot forward and lower your body until both knees are bent at approximately 90 degrees — your front knee should be over your ankle and your back knee hovering just above the floor. Push through the heel of your front foot to return to the start position, then repeat on the other side. Lunges develop unilateral leg strength and challenge balance and coordination.
Lunges with Weights: Hold a dumbbell in each hand by your sides and perform a standard lunge. Step one foot forward and lower into the lunge position, keeping your torso upright and core engaged. The added weight increases the resistance on the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. Step back to the start and alternate legs. Keep the weights controlled and avoid swinging them as you step.
Lunges with weights: Hold a dumbbell in each hand by your sides and perform a standard lunge. Step one foot forward and lower into the lunge position, keeping your torso upright and core engaged. The added weight increases the resistance on the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. Step back to the start and alternate legs. Keep the weights controlled and avoid swinging them as you step.
Reverse Lunges: Stand tall with your feet together and, if using weights, a dumbbell in each hand. Step one foot backward and lower your body until both knees are at 90 degrees — your front knee stays over your ankle. Push through the front heel to return to the start position. Reverse lunges place less stress on the knee joint compared to forward lunges while still effectively targeting the glutes, hamstrings, and quads. Alternate legs each rep.
Standing Calf Raises: Stand on the edge of a step or flat floor with your feet hip-width apart. Rise up onto the balls of your feet by pressing through your toes and contracting your calf muscles. Hold at the top for a moment, then slowly lower your heels back down — drop below the step level if possible for a full stretch. Calf raises target the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles of the lower leg. Hold dumbbells for added resistance.
Roller: Use a foam roller to apply sustained pressure to a targeted muscle group by resting the muscle on the roller and using your body weight. Slowly roll along the muscle belly, pausing on any particularly tight or tender spots for 20-30 seconds to allow the tissue to release. Common areas include the IT band, quads, hamstrings, calves, and upper back. Foam rolling helps improve tissue quality, reduce soreness, and increase range of motion.
